lesson.title: When Both Go Up Together: Positive Correlation
lesson.summary: Positive correlation means that as one variable increases, the other variable also tends to increase, shown on a scatterplot as points that generally rise from the lower left toward the upper right.
lesson.body:
Positive correlation is the specific case of correlation where larger x-values tend to pair with larger y-values. On a scatterplot, this shows up as points that generally drift from the lower left corner of the graph toward the upper right corner. This is the same rising pattern seen in the hours-studied and test-score example from the previous chapters.

Here is a worked example. Comparing the shoe size and height of five people gives the paired data set (7, 62), (8, 64), (9, 66), (10, 68), (11, 70), where x is shoe size and y is height in inches. Each time shoe size increases by 1, height increases by exactly 2 inches: 62 to 64 to 66 to 68 to 70. That is a clear, consistent rising pattern from lower left to upper right, so this data set shows a positive correlation, and because every single step matches so exactly, it counts as an unusually strong positive correlation.

Positive correlation itself comes in different strengths. A strong positive correlation has points that hug closely to a rising trend, like the shoe size and height example just plotted. A weak positive correlation still trends generally upward overall, but the points are scattered more loosely around that rising trend rather than following it precisely, showing the same direction with far less consistency.

One last reminder, worth repeating every time: positive correlation only describes a pattern observed in data, it does not explain why that pattern exists. A larger shoe size does not cause a person to be taller. Both shoe size and height tend to result from a person's overall physical growth, a separate underlying factor. Recognizing positive correlation is a useful descriptive tool for spotting and naming a relationship hiding in a data set, but the explanation behind that relationship always requires more information than a scatterplot alone can ever provide.
